processing: The dried ripe seed of the malva nut tree is rinsed and soaked in boiling water, where its middle coat swells into a spongy mass. Nothing else is done to it beyond drying.
harvest_season: Sold year-round as a dried herbal seed; harvest timing is not a selling point.
appearance_dry: Spindle-shaped or oval brown seed, 2 to 3 cm long, with a slight sheen and irregular wrinkles.
appearance_liquor: Clear, soft yellow to light amber, with a slightly slippery body.
appearance_wet: Swollen into a large, loose brown sponge that breaks apart in the cup.
taste_profile: Mild and smooth, with a slippery texture and little aroma; many people add a bit of sugar.

brewing.notes: Rinse one or two seeds in warm water, put them in a cup with a lid, pour on boiling water and leave covered. Trimming both ends first helps them open.

vintage_note: Sold as dried seeds by weight with no harvest year. Trade grades rank plump, full, intact seeds highest, while flatter, shrunken ones come lower. Keep them cool and dry, since light, damp and warmth spoil them.
description:
Pangdahai cha is a folk throat remedy rather than a tea to enjoy: the dried seed of the malva nut tree, Sterculia lychnophora, soaked in boiling water. Its charm is watching a wrinkled seed swell into a big brown sponge.

There is no real processing beyond drying. The swelling comes from the seed's middle coat, which is why the name means roughly fat big sea and why shops also call it da hai or dafa.

The cup is gentle, smooth and slightly slippery, with hardly any fragrance. Teachers, singers and smokers are the classic drinkers in China, using it for a hoarse, dry throat. Use one or two seeds, not a handful, as they expand a great deal.

This is a herbal medicine, so treat it as one. Chinese herbal guidance says it should not be an everyday drink, suggests no more than about seven days in a row, and warns off people with weak digestion, a cold from chills, low blood pressure or diabetes. A persistent sore throat deserves a doctor.

When buying, go for full, round seeds with a clean smell and no mould. Quoted grades exist, but they are trade categories rather than a formal standard.
history: The seed's medicinal use is first recorded in Ben Cao Gang Mu Shi Yi, the Qing-era supplement to the Compendium of Materia Medica. It remains a known folk remedy in China for hoarseness and sore throat. One of its old names, An Nan Zi, refers to Annam, but little is documented about how it first entered the Chinese herbal trade.
